Central Nervous System
Anatomy
Mandibular Nerve

Quick Overview

The mandibular nerve (V3) is the third and largest division of the trigeminal nerve, formed by a large sensory root and a small motor root. It leaves the skull through the foramen ovale into the infratemporal fossa and divides into anterior and posterior divisions. This lesson covers its trunk branches, the mostly motor anterior division, and the mostly sensory posterior division (auriculotemporal, lingual, and inferior alveolar nerves).

Complete Lesson Content

General Features

  • Largest, third division of the fifth cranial nerve (trigeminal nerve, V).
  • Roots: a large sensory root and a small motor root.
  • Leaves the cranial cavity through the foramen ovale to enter the infratemporal fossa.
  • Trunk: short, lying deep to the lateral pterygoid.
  • Divisions: divides shortly into anterior and posterior divisions.

Branches from the Trunk

  1. Nervus spinosus: passes through the foramen spinosum and supplies the dura mater.
  2. Nerve to medial pterygoid: also gives a branch to the tensor palati and the tensor tympani muscles.
  3. Motor root to the otic ganglion (nerve supply to the parotid salivary gland), passing via the nerve to medial pterygoid and lying medial to the mandibular nerve trunk.

Anterior Division

Motor, except for the buccal nerve. Branches:

  • Branch to the masseter.
  • Two or three branches to the temporalis.
  • Branch to the lateral pterygoid.
  • Buccal nerve (sensory): to the mucous membrane of the cheek.

Posterior Division

The posterior division is sensory, except for the nerve to mylohyoid (motor).

NerveCourseSupply / Function
Auriculotemporal (sensory)Arises by two roots that surround the middle meningeal artery. Passes backward deep to the neck of the mandible into the parotid gland and emerges from its upper end.Sensory to the scalp in front of the auricle. Carries postganglionic parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland.
LingualJoined by the chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve. The submandibular ganglion is attached to it in the submandibular fossa.General sensation from the anterior two thirds of the tongue. Carries postganglionic parasympathetic fibers to the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands. Chorda tympani carries taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue.
Inferior alveolarPasses through the mandibular foramen into the mandibular canal; emerges from the mental foramen as the mental nerve.Gives the nerve to mylohyoid, which runs in the mylohyoid groove and supplies the mylohyoid and the anterior belly of digastric.

Key Points / Quick Review

Overview

  • V3 = largest division of the trigeminal; sensory + motor roots.
  • Exits via foramen ovale into the infratemporal fossa.
  • Short trunk deep to lateral pterygoid, then anterior and posterior divisions.

Trunk

  • Nervus spinosus (foramen spinosum): dura.
  • Nerve to medial pterygoid: also tensor palati and tensor tympani.
  • Motor root to the otic ganglion (parotid).

Anterior division

  • Motor: masseter, temporalis, lateral pterygoid.
  • Only sensory branch: buccal nerve (cheek mucosa).

Posterior division

  • Sensory except nerve to mylohyoid.
  • Auriculotemporal: scalp in front of auricle; parasympathetic to parotid.
  • Lingual: general sensation of anterior two thirds of the tongue; joined by chorda tympani (taste, parasympathetic to submandibular and sublingual glands).
  • Inferior alveolar: mandibular canal, mental nerve; nerve to mylohyoid supplies mylohyoid and anterior belly of digastric.
